passage: Sunday, late. I've been sick with fever all week, and today was the first day I went to school. Everything felt heavy, even my bag. I walked so slowly that Parveen had to wait at the gate twice. In the class my eyes kept closing and when Rohit asked me for my ruler, I snapped, "Get your own!" I felt bad right after. Amma says I need lots of sleep and no big homework for a few days. She made khichdi and let me lie on the sofa. I feel a little better now. If I'm still this tired next week, Amma says we'll ask the doctor. — Imran

qa.q: Who waited at the gate twice for Imran?
qa.a: Parveen waited at the gate twice.

qa.q: Why did Imran snap at Rohit, and what does Imran say about feeling afterwards?
qa.a: Imran was worn out after being ill, so snapped easily. Imran felt bad right after, which shows the snap was tiredness and not meanness.

qa.q: What could Imran's family do to help Imran recover?
qa.a: Give Imran rest and low demands, as Amma does, and check with the doctor if the tiredness goes on.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel about waiting for Imran?
qa.a: Parveen waited at the gate twice, so is probably patient and caring, and might also be worried about how slow and heavy Imran looks.

grounding: A school-age child after illness looks drained, moves slowly and snaps easily; weariness needs rest and low demands, and lasting exhaustion calls for checking health.

passage: The harvest week at Amandeep's family farm went on until dark every day. Chandrika, ten, had helped carry sacks since morning. By the fifth evening she was moving as if underwater, dragging her feet and rubbing her eyes. Amandeep, her cousin, asked her to fetch the water pail and she snapped, "You do it, I'm tired!" He looked surprised. Chandrika sat on the step and put her chin in her hands. Her mother saw her and said, "Enough for today. Eat, then sleep." Chandrika didn't argue. Later Amandeep brought her a glass of milk and didn't say anything about the snap.

qa.q: What did Chandrika drag as she moved?
qa.a: She dragged her feet.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika snap at Amandeep, and what else could be behind her reaction?
qa.a: She was tired after days of work and snapped without meaning to. If this tiredness kept up, it might point to something else, like sleep or stress, that needs a check.

qa.q: What could the family do to help Chandrika after the harvest week?
qa.a: Let her rest with fewer chores, make sure she gets enough sleep, and check with a doctor if the tiredness lasts.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel after Chandrika's snap?
qa.a: He was surprised but brought her milk and said nothing, so he seems to understand she was worn out.

grounding: A school-age child after long days of work looks drained, moves slowly and snaps easily; rest and low demands help.

passage:
Rafael came home from the all-day football tournament in Lisbon with mud up to his knees. He dropped his bag in the hall and didn't pick it up. He walked slowly, as if his shoes were made of stone.
His little sister Amara ran at him with her drawing. "Rafa, look! Look!"
"Not now!" he snapped, and she stepped back, lip trembling.
Their mother saw his grey face. She didn't ask about homework. "Shower, then soup, then bed," she said gently. "Amara, show him tomorrow."
After the shower Rafael sat at the table, eating slowly. Then he called Amara over. "Sorry. Show me now, quickly." He looked at the drawing and managed a tired smile.

qa.q: What did Rafael do with his bag?
qa.a: He dropped it in the hall and didn't pick it up.

qa.q: Why did Rafael snap at Amara?
qa.a: He felt worn out and drained after the long tournament, so even a small demand made him irritable rather than angry at her.

qa.q: What did the mother do that matched Rafael's weariness?
qa.a: She lowered demands by skipping homework and gave him a simple plan of shower, soup and bed.

qa.q: How might Amara have felt when Rafael snapped?
qa.a: Amara probably felt hurt and confused, since she only wanted to share her drawing.

grounding: After a long tournament, a child looks drained, moves slowly and snaps, and a parent responds with rest and low demands.

passage:
Shreya was back at school after a week of fever. She walked slowly up the stairs, holding the rail. In class she rested her head on her arm between lessons.
When Asif asked to borrow her eraser for the third time, she snapped, "Can't you get your own?"
Asif looked stung.
Mrs Menon, the class teacher, noticed. At break she said, "Shreya, you look very tired. You don't have to do PT today, and you can finish the worksheet at home." She let Shreya sit in the library corner.
After school, Mrs Menon told Shreya's mother about the tiredness, and her mother said they would check with the doctor if it kept going.

qa.q: Where did Mrs Menon let Shreya sit at break?
qa.a: In the library corner.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she snapped at Asif?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and irritable after being ill, so even a small request felt like too much.

qa.q: What did Mrs Menon do that helped Shreya?
qa.a: She lowered demands, excused PT, gave her a quiet place to rest, and told her mother about the tiredness.

qa.q: How might Asif see Shreya's snapping?
qa.a: Asif probably felt hurt and surprised, not realising she was still tired from being sick.

grounding: A child returning after illness looks drained and snaps, and a teacher offers rest, low demands and a check with family.

passage:
My cousin Pallavi has been tired for weeks. She falls asleep on the sofa after school, doesn't want to play badminton any more, and yesterday she snapped at her mother just for asking about her day.
I heard her say she stays up late finishing homework and then can't sleep because she's worried about the exams.
Her mother sat with her last night. "You've been tired for a long time, beta. Let's look at your sleep and your worries. And we'll see the doctor this week."
Pallavi cried a little. I think she was relieved someone noticed.
Today she went to bed early, and her mother helped her make a homework plan.
- Vishal

qa.q: What sport does Pallavi not want to play any more?
qa.a: Badminton.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have been feeling when she cried?
qa.a: She was probably relieved that someone noticed how tired and stressed she was, though Vishal can't be sure.

qa.q: What steps did Pallavi's mother take for the long tiredness?
qa.a: She talked with Pallavi, looked at her sleep and worries, planned a doctor's visit, and helped her plan homework.

qa.q: How did Vishal experience seeing Pallavi so tired?
qa.a: Vishal noticed the changes and seemed concerned, watching closely and glad someone was helping.

grounding: An observer sees a child with lasting exhaustion, and a parent checks sleep, health and stress.

passage:
Monday: It was Jaya's first day back at school after her fever. She walked home slowly, dragging her bag. When Noor from next door called, "Come and play langdi!", Jaya snapped, "Leave me alone!" and shut the door. Then she lay on the sofa with her shoes still on.
Tuesday: Amma cancelled Jaya's tuition for the week and let her skip chores. Jaya slept early. In the morning she knocked on Noor's door. "Sorry I shouted. I was so tired." Noor shrugged. "I thought you were cross with me."
Two weeks later: Jaya was still yawning through the afternoons and had stopped wanting to play at all. Amma watched her closely, then took her to the family doctor to check her sleep and whether anything else was wrong.

qa.q: What game did Noor call Jaya to play?
qa.a: Langdi.

qa.q: Why did Jaya snap at Noor on Monday?
qa.a: Jaya felt drained and exhausted after the fever, with nothing left for play, so the invitation felt like too much.

qa.q: What did Amma do as Jaya's tiredness went on?
qa.a: First she gave rest and fewer demands; when the weariness lasted and Jaya stopped wanting to play, she took her to the doctor to check sleep and health.

qa.q: How did Noor read Jaya's snapping?
qa.a: Noor thought Jaya was cross with her, not that Jaya was simply worn out.

grounding: It shows a school-age child drained after illness, moving slowly and snapping, needing rest and low demands, and a check-up when the exhaustion lasts.
